title: Lab 4:Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
1.Load packages and prepare the setup


Code
library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom.mixed)
library(performance)
library(gt)
library(readr)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(titanic)
library(psych)

titanic <- titanic_train



Keep the same complete-case sample for every model


Code
titanic <- titanic |>
  select(Survived, Sex, Age, Pclass) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    Sex.Binary = case_when(
      Sex == "male" ~ 0,
      Sex == "female" ~ 1)) |>
  mutate(
    Survived.Char = case_when(
      Survived == 0 ~ "Died",
      Survived == 1 ~ "Survived")) |>
  mutate(
    Pclass.Char = case_when(
      Pclass == "1" ~ "First Class",
      Pclass == "2" ~ "Second Class",
      Pclass == "3" ~ "Third Class")) |>
  mutate(Pclass = factor(Pclass, levels = c(1, 2, 3))) |>
  select(Survived, Survived.Char, Sex, Sex.Binary, Pclass, Pclass.Char, Age)

title: Lab 4:Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
2.1. Prediction
I expect sex, ticket class, and age to be associated with survival. Female passengers may have been more likely to survive because the “women and children first” principle may have given them priority when boarding lifeboats. I also expect first-class passengers to have higher survival probabilities than second- and third-class passengers, because their accommodation may have provided easier access to lifeboats and shorter evacuation routes. Finally, I expect younger passengers to have higher survival probabilities because children may have received priority and assistance from adults during the evacuation.

title: Lab 4:Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
section: 2.2. Specify four nested binary logistic regression models
text:
2.2. Specify four nested binary logistic regression models


Code
# Model 0: Intercept-only model
mod0 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ 1,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic
)

# Model 1: Add sex (0 = male, 1 = female)
mod1 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic
)

# Model 2: Add ticket class (reference = first class)
mod2 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic
)

# Model 3: Add age (in years)
mod3 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass + Age,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic
)

section: 3.3. Combine model-performance statistics and nested-model tests

title: Lab 4:Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
Create the model-comparison table
Among the four candidate models, mod3, which included sex, ticket class, and age, provided the best balance between fit and complexity, with the lowest AIC (657.28) and BIC (680.14). Both criteria decreased at each step as predictors were added. Likelihood-ratio tests showed that adding sex improved fit over the null model, χ²(1) = 213.82; adding ticket class improved fit beyond sex, χ²(2) = 78.27; and adding age further improved fit beyond sex and ticket class, χ²(1) = 25.15 (all p < .001). Thus, AIC, BIC, and the likelihood-ratio tests supported the same conclusion: each addition improved fit enough to justify the extra model complexity. Sex contributed beyond the baseline model, ticket class contributed beyond sex, and age contributed beyond both. These comparisons support mod3 as the leading candidate, subject to diagnostic checks.


Code
model_comparison |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Binary Logistic Regression Models",
    subtitle = paste("Complete-case sample: N =", nrow(titanic))
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    residual_df = "Residual df",

title: Lab 4:Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
4.1. Examine the assumptions
The DHARMa diagnostics showed no significant overall deviations from residual uniformity, dispersion, or the expected frequency of simulation outliers. Residual patterns across age were broadly flat, providing no clear evidence against the linear age term on the logit scale. No significant residual problems were detected across sex. However, residual variability differed significantly across ticket classes, although within-class uniformity tests were not significant. This suggests a possible class-specific lack of fit and warrants caution when interpreting class-related estimates and predicted probabilities. Overall, the residual diagnostics broadly support retaining mod3, while indicating that its fit is not equally adequate across all ticket classes.


Code
candidate_model <- mod3

# Generate reproducible simulated residuals
sim_res <- DHARMa::simulateResiduals(
  fittedModel = candidate_model,
  n = 1000,
  seed = 9041
)

# Overall diagnostic plots
plot(sim_res)











Code
# Examine residual patterns across age
DHARMa::plotResiduals(
  sim_res,
  form = titanic$Age
)









Code
# Examine residual patterns across categorical predictors
DHARMa::plotResiduals(
  sim_res,
  form = factor(titanic$Sex.Binary)
)









Code
DHARMa::plotResiduals(
  sim_res,
  form = titanic$Pclass
)

title: Lab 4:Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
5.1. Select a model
I selected mod3, which includes sex, ticket class, and age, as the preferred model. It had the lowest AIC (657.28) and BIC (680.14), indicating the best balance between fit and complexity among the four candidates. The nested likelihood-ratio tests supported each addition of predictors; importantly, adding age improved fit beyond sex and ticket class, χ²(1) = 25.15, p <0.001. Thus, the simpler models omit predictors that contribute additional information about survival. The included predictors also have clear substantive interpretations related to evacuation priority and access to lifeboats, although these mechanisms were not directly tested. Overall DHARMa diagnostics and residual patterns across age were broadly reassuring. However, differences in simulated residual variability across ticket classes suggest possible local lack of fit, so class-related estimates and predicted probabilities should be interpreted cautiously.


Code
preferred_model <- mod3
formula(preferred_model)

title: Lab 4:Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
5.5. Overarching summary
Binary logistic regression was used to examine associations between sex, ticket class, age, and survival among 714 passengers. Of the four candidate models, the model including all three predictors was preferred based on AIC, BIC, and nested likelihood-ratio tests. It also improved fit over the intercept-only model, χ²(4) = 317.23, p <0.001. Adjusting for the other predictors, females had 12.46 times the odds of survival of males (95% CI [8.30, 18.71]). Relative to first-class passengers, the odds ratios were 0.27 for second-class passengers (95% CI [0.16, 0.47]) and 0.08 for third-class passengers (95% CI [0.04, 0.13]). Each additional year of age was associated with lower survival odds (OR = 0.964, 95% CI [0.949, 0.978]). These findings were consistent with the predicted advantages for female, first-class, and younger passengers. However, class-specific residual differences warrant caution, and these observational associations do not establish the mechanisms responsible for survival.

title: Lab 4:Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
section: 5.6. Visualize age and predicted survival probability
text:
5.6. Visualize age and predicted survival probability
For male passengers in first class, predicted survival probability decreased with age. The shaded band represents uncertainty around the estimated probability. Although age enters the model linearly on the logit scale, its association with survival probability is curved. These predictions apply to the specified sex and ticket class rather than representing an average across all passengers.


Code
# Generate predicted survival probabilities across age
age_predictions <- ggeffects::ggpredict(
  preferred_model,
  terms = "Age [all]",
  condition = c(
    Sex.Binary = 0,
    Pclass = "1"
  )
) |>
  as.data.frame()

# Plot predicted probabilities and 95% confidence intervals
ggplot(age_predictions, aes(x = x, y = predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
    fill = "#669BBC",
    alpha = 0.20
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#2C5F7C",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age and Predicted Survival Probability",
    subtitle = "Predictions for male passengers in first class",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Predicted probability of survival",
    caption = "Shaded band represents the 95% confidence interval."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
